entries.clue: Balls being inverted, used glue – overwhelming amount (6)

indicators.note: to invert something is to turn it upside down, so the two letters from Balls come out back to front
glue that has been used has been worked and smeared about, so its letters no longer sit in their original order

blocks.note: Ed Balls, the former Labour minister, supplies ED, turned round

annotation.surface: A slapstick picture of someone upside down in a pot of glue, with a flood of trouble to follow.
annotation.walkthrough: In a Private Eye puzzle 'Balls' looks like the usual smut, but it is Ed Balls, the Labour politician turned TV personality, who gives ED.
annotation.definitionFit: Figurative sense: a deluge is literally a flood, and by extension any overwhelming amount, as in a deluge of complaints.

entries.clue: Tension relaxer produced by CID employee cut by criminal teen (7)

indicators.note: a word that is cut has been shortened, so DETECTIVE loses its tail and becomes DET
criminal means bent or crooked, so the letters of TEEN are bent out of order

blocks.note: a CID employee is a DETECTIVE, cut short

annotation.surface: A police report: a detective knifed by a young offender.
annotation.walkthrough: The CID is the Criminal Investigation Department of a British police force, so its employee is a detective. 'Cut by' reads as stabbed, but 'cut' shortens the detective and 'by' just places the next piece beside him.
annotation.definitionFit: Descriptive definition: détente is the easing of hostility between nations, the thing that relaxes international tension.

entries.clue: 'Light unit' initially unveiled at Rio and America: suitable for the Sunaks' lifestyle? (9)

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of unveiled is used

blocks.note: the lux is the SI unit of illumination

annotation.surface: A product launch unveiled in Rio and America, pitched at the very rich.
annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'Light unit' look like a product name, but it is a physics unit. Rishi Sunak, the former Prime Minister, and his wife Akshata Murty are famously wealthy, hence the question mark.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the Sunaks' wealthy way of life is a case of the sumptuous comfort the answer describes.

entries.clue: Gum extremely flabby with teeth protruding (5)

indicators.note: extremely is read as 'at the extremes', so only the two end letters of flabby are taken

annotation.surface: An unflattering dental description: slack gums and buck teeth.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gum' sits next to teeth, so it looks like part of the mouth, but it is the sticky substance.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal sense: goofy teeth are buck teeth, ones that stick out.

entries.clue: Piss taken at the doctor's? (8)

blocks.note: the surface reading is mockery, since taking the piss is British slang for making fun of someone; the setter means urine literally collected
the place where a urine sample is handed over for testing

annotation.surface: Sounds like someone being mocked at the GP's surgery.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: the question mark flags that 'piss taken' should be read literally rather than as the slang for mockery.
annotation.definitionFit: Cryptic definition: a urine sample collected by a doctor for testing is known as a specimen.

entries.clue: State staff finally ready to take the piss (6)

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the closing letter of ready is used

annotation.surface: The employees of some state are finally poised to mock someone.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Staff' reads as employees, but it is a stick. Take the piss is British slang for to mock.
annotation.definitionFit: Slang equivalent: to parody someone is to mock them by imitation, which in British slang is taking the piss.

entries.clue: Adversary makes political party sore (9)

annotation.surface: An opponent leaves a political party smarting.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sore' reads as annoyed, which suits a party upset by a rival, but it means physically tender.
annotation.definitionFit: Near synonym: a rival competing against you in a contest is your adversary.

entries.clue: Muck – there's a lot surrounding Labour leader (5)

indicators.note: surrounding means lying all around something, so the word for 'a lot' is placed on both sides of the leader's letter

annotation.surface: A jibe that the Labour leader is surrounded by plenty of dirt.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Labour leader' looks like the party's head, but it is only the first letter of Labour.
annotation.definitionFit: Loose synonym: mulch is rotting organic matter spread over soil, the sort of stuff a gardener would call muck.

entries.clue: Negative Poles peak without a break (3-4)

blocks.note: N and S, the north and south poles

annotation.surface: Gloomy Polish climbers head for the summit without resting.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Poles' looks like people from Poland; in crosswords it usually gives the two poles, N and S.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: continuing with no pause or interruption.

entries.clue: Biden's son in the view of some Republicans: "Corrupt detox grad!" (3,6)

definitions.text: Biden's son in the view of some Republicans

indicators.note: corrupt means spoilt or twisted from its proper form, so the letters of the phrase are twisted into a new order

annotation.surface: A Republican jeer at Hunter Biden as a crooked graduate of rehab.
annotation.walkthrough: Hunter Biden, son of President Joe Biden, went through addiction treatment and was charged over unpaid taxes, so both the fodder and the answer belong to the Republican attack on him.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: Republicans accused Hunter Biden of evading his taxes, so this is what they called him.

entries.clue: Try sand to shift balls (6)

indicators.note: to shift something is to move it about, so the letters of sand are moved into a new order

blocks.note: have a go = have a try

annotation.surface: Advice to have a go at moving sand, perhaps so the balls on a beach pitch roll better.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Balls' at the end reads as sports equipment on the sand, but it is the slang for testicles.
annotation.definitionFit: Slang equivalent: gonads are the sex glands, and balls is slang for the male ones.

entries.clue: Material only about Biden's end (5)

indicators.note: about can mean around and about, in a different arrangement, so the letters are moved round
the end of Biden is its closing letter

annotation.surface: A report that the only relevant material concerns the end of Biden's career.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Material' reads as relevant information, but it is a fabric.
annotation.definitionFit: Hypernym: nylon is a synthetic fabric, one kind of material.

entries.clue: Deny bust covers bottom of jumper, like a geek (5)

indicators.note: something bust is broken, so the letters of deny are broken up and reassembled
to cover something is to lie over it on all sides, so the rearranged letters go around the R
the bottom of a word is its final letter

annotation.surface: Someone insists they don't look geeky, even though their bust hangs over the bottom of their jumper.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bust' looks like a chest, which fits the jumper, but it means broken. A jumper is British for a sweater.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a nerd is a geek, so the adjective describes someone geekish.

entries.clue: It's grand to break into naked jog (5)

indicators.note: a burglar who breaks into a house ends up inside it, so the G goes inside the word for naked

annotation.surface: Someone declares that it would be great to set off on a naked run.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Grand' reads as 'great', and 'jog' as running, which suit a streaker; they are G for a thousand pounds and a gentle push.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: to jog someone's elbow is to give it a small push.

entries.clue: (& 24ac.) Latest advice bound to restrict Times and Independent (3)

indicators.note: to restrict something is to hem it in, so the word for bound holds the newspaper letters inside it

blocks.note: T = time, doubled for the plural

annotation.surface: A tip-off that new rules are set to muzzle two national newspapers, The Times and The Independent.
annotation.walkthrough: The capitals make Times and Independent look like the newspapers; they are just the abbreviations T and I. The answer runs on into 24 across.
annotation.definitionFit: Idiom: a hot tip is a piece of fresh, inside information, the newest guidance on offer.

entries.clue: Early Viking leaders loved balls getting developed (7)

indicators.note: the leaders of words are their first letters, taken from Early and Viking
to balls something up is to make a mess of it, so the letters of loved are jumbled

blocks.note: first letters of Early and Viking

annotation.surface: A cheeky history note: the first Viking chiefs loved balls, and the game grew from there.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Balls' reads as a noun the leaders loved, but it is a verb, as in to balls up, and it scrambles LOVED.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: something that has evolved has grown or developed gradually.

entries.clue: You've tangled with Mrs I. looking for sexual arousal (9)

indicators.note: tangled threads are twisted into knots, so these letters are twisted into a new order

annotation.surface: An accusation that you have been messing about with a married woman out of lust.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tangled with' reads as having an affair with Mrs I., which suits the sexual theme, but it scrambles the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Descriptive definition: voyeurism is gaining sexual pleasure from watching others, looking in order to be aroused.

entries.clue: Lose erection (dead poor circulation) (5)

indicators.note: things in circulation move around, so the letters of poor move into a new order

blocks.note: d = dead, as in family trees

annotation.surface: A medical note: impotence caused by bad blood flow.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is real medicine, since poor circulation does cause impotence, which is why 'circulation' is hard to spot as an instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Descriptive definition: to lose an erection is to go limp and sag.

entries.clue: Outlaw's corset is tight with article concealed (9)

indicators.note: tight is slang for drunk, so the letters stagger into a new order
something concealed is hidden inside, so the article is tucked in among the other letters

annotation.surface: A bandit's corset is laced tight, with some item smuggled inside it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tight' reads as a description of the laced corset, but it means drunk.
annotation.definitionFit: Verb synonym: to outlaw someone is to cast them out of society, to exclude them.

entries.clue: Who won't stand for a drunken spree? (6)

blocks.note: someone who bends rather than standing up straight
British slang for a long session of heavy drinking

annotation.surface: Asks who would refuse to put up with a drinking binge.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Won't stand for' reads as won't tolerate, but 'for' is only a link: the first sense is literally one who bends instead of standing.
annotation.definitionFit: Double definition: one who bends is literally a bender, and in British slang the word also means a drinking binge.

entries.clue: Hard up lead broadcaster sounding croaky (5)

indicators.note: the lead is what goes in front, so only the first letter of up is used

annotation.surface: A lead presenter, short of money, with a croaky voice.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hard up' looks like a phrase meaning broke, but it splits into H and the first letter of up.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a husky voice is low and hoarse, sounding rough in the throat.

entries.clue: Snag on being married: wife leaves – to get married (7)

definitions.note: the definition works in the phrase 'to get hitched'

indicators.note: when someone leaves they are no longer there, so W for wife goes out of the word

annotation.surface: A wedding goes wrong when the wife walks out, and yet they still marry.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Married' appears twice: the first is wordplay for WED, the last is part of the definition. Getting hitched is informal for getting married.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal idiom: a hitch joins a horse to a cart, so a couple who are hitched have been joined together in marriage.

entries.clue: Shifting Carter involved one's being on the inside (7)

indicators.note: involved means complicated or twisted, so the letters of Carter are twisted into a new order
the letter for one is placed within the others

annotation.surface: A Carter is mixed up in some shifty business, with someone on the inside.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Involved' reads as implicated in a crime, which suits 'on the inside', but it means twisted, the anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: something erratic is irregular and keeps changing unpredictably.

entries.clue: Name implicated in sneaky reform (7)

indicators.note: to be implicated in something is to be caught up inside it, so the N sits within the word for sneaky

annotation.surface: Someone is named as involved in an underhand reform.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Reform' reads as a noun, a policy change, but the definition is the verb, to change someone's ways.
annotation.definitionFit: Verb synonym: to reform a sinner is to change their beliefs or habits for the better.

entries.clue: Very dull duke (English) put in list (6)

indicators.note: to be put in something is to be placed inside it, so D and E go into the word for list

annotation.surface: A tedious English duke gets added to a list.
annotation.walkthrough: 'List' looks like a roll of names, but it is the verb, to tilt over as a ship does.
annotation.definitionFit: Figurative sense: lead is heavy and grey, so leaden prose or skies are heavy and dreary.

entries.clue: see 14ac. (3)
Censure one Conservative and cause alarm (5)

blocks.note: to pan is to criticise harshly

annotation.surface: Attacking a Tory and stirring up alarm.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Censure' reads as a formal rebuke, but it is PAN, as a critic pans a play.
annotation.definitionFit: Verb sense: as a transitive verb it means to throw someone into sudden fear.

entries.clue: Stupendous housing tip (5)

indicators.note: a building housing something holds it inside, so the answer is held inside the first word

blocks.note: the letters after ST and before OUS

annotation.surface: A marvellous tip-off about a house.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tip' looks like advice, as in the 14/24 answer, but here it is the verb, to tip over.
annotation.definitionFit: Verb synonym: to tip a thing over is to turn it on its end.

entries.clue: Start of Trump's downfall – and retinue (5)

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: rain is a downfall from the sky

annotation.surface: The beginning of Trump's ruin, dragging his hangers-on down too.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Downfall' reads as political ruin, but it is rain falling down.
annotation.definitionFit: Collective noun: a train is the body of attendants following an important person.

entries.clue: Silent air-conditioning installed in Bristol (5)

indicators.note: equipment installed in a building is fitted inside it, so the air-conditioning letters go inside the Bristol word

annotation.surface: A quiet air-conditioning unit fitted in a building in Bristol, the English city.
annotation.walkthrough: Bristols is Cockney rhyming slang for breasts, from Bristol City, the football club, so one Bristol gives TIT.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: tacit agreement is unspoken, given silently.

entries.clue: Hospital needs a number one – and capital (5)

blocks.note: H = hospital, as on road signs

annotation.surface: A hospital wants a top person in charge, and money.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Number one' reads as a boss, and 'capital' as money, but they split into NO and I, and capital is a capital city.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the city is the capital of Vietnam.

entries.clue: "One has to follow Blunt's command" (9)

indicators.note: to follow is to come after, so the piece for 'one has' is placed after the word for blunt

annotation.surface: A quotation from a pompous order: someone must obey a person called Blunt.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Blunt' looks like a surname, perhaps the spy Anthony Blunt, but it means frank.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a directive is an official instruction that must be obeyed.

entries.clue: For the record, desist from wrapping rod round Mordaunt's head! (8)

indicators.note: a wrapping goes all round what it holds, so the word for desist goes round everything else
round means encircling, so the word for rod encircles the M
the head of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: a cue is the rod used in snooker

annotation.surface: A warning, on the record, to stop beating the Tory MP Penny Mordaunt about the head with a stick.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For the record' looks like the definition, but only 'record' is, used as a verb. Penny Mordaunt is a Conservative MP; she only supplies her initial.
annotation.definitionFit: Verb synonym: to record something is to set it down in writing as evidence.

entries.clue: Act like a witness going topless – most gross! (6)

indicators.note: going topless means losing the top, so the first letter is removed

blocks.note: gross = fat, so most gross = fattest

annotation.surface: A witness strips to the waist, to universal disgust.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Topless' suggests a Page Three scene, but it just drops the first letter. 'Gross' reads as disgusting, but here it means fat.
annotation.definitionFit: Descriptive definition: a witness bears formal testimony that something is true.
